The famous ship that sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg was the RMS Titanic.

In an alternative ending, as Clara stepped into the contraption, she noticed a slight misalignment in the blade mechanism that had been hidden from her during rehearsals. Instead of proceeding with the dangerous leap, she paused, her heart pounding not just from fear but from sudden clarity. She realized that true mastery wasn't about defying death, but about understanding the mechanics of illusion so deeply that one could control the outcome. With a calm breath, she signaled the stagehand to halt the performance. The audience murmured in confusion, but Clara stepped out of the machine, bowed gracefully, and announced that the greatest magic was not in the risk, but in the wisdom to know when to stop. Her career did not end in disgrace; instead, it evolved into a celebrated exploration of psychological illusion, earning her respect as a pioneer who valued artistry over spectacle.
